overview: Vijayanagara, founded on the Tungabhadra in 1336, ruled the south of India for three centuries and made its capital, today's Hampi, one of the largest cities in the world. It kept the temple culture of the Tamil and Kannada country alive and traded horses and spices with the Portuguese, the Arabs and China.

items.text: Gopurams, towered gateways, and pillared halls carried Dravidian temple building to its most elaborate.
Under Krishnadevaraya (1509 to 1529) the Krishna temple was built at Hampi and the Vittala temple gained its stone chariot and musical pillars.
Krishnadevaraya kept eight Telugu poets at court and wrote the Amuktamalyada himself; Kannada, Tamil and Sanskrit letters flourished too.
Arab and Portuguese traders sold the warhorses the empire needed; Hampi's markets sold diamonds, spices and cloth.
The Portuguese Domingo Paes, who saw the city about 1520, called it as large as Rome and the best provided city in the world.
Estimates of the capital's people run to several hundred thousand, among the largest cities of the sixteenth century.
Canals from the Tungabhadra and large tanks watered the fields around the city.
The Group of Monuments at Hampi was listed by UNESCO; more than 1,600 remains survive.
The empire's temple styles and its Nayaka successors kept Hindu kingship alive in the south.

fall.text: The Deccan sultanates crushed the imperial army at Talikota in 1565 and sacked the capital. The Aravidu kings ruled a shrinking realm from Penukonda, Chandragiri and Vellore until Bijapur and Golconda took the last of it in 1646.

sources.title: UNESCO, Group of Monuments at Hampi
